title: Three-pair Directed Edge Multicut
formal: Is three-pair Directed Edge Multicut fixed-parameter tractable, allowing randomization, with the number of deleted arcs as parameter? Precisely, does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm, a total computable function \(h:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and a constant \(c\ge1\), such that every input \((D,(s_i,t_i)_{i=1}^3,k)\) is processed in at most \(h(k)(n+1)^c\) bit steps for every random tape, the algorithm never returns an invalid cut, and, whenever a cut of size at most \(k\) exists, it returns one with probability at least \(2/3\)? This historical question has an affirmative answer in the SODA 2023 result cited below.
why: A single directed separation demand is a minimum-cut problem, while several demands can share deleted arcs in complicated ways. Fixing only three demands isolates the last small-pair case left between established tractability and hardness results. The published resolution determines this boundary for the unweighted cardinality parameter.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively by the checked SODA 2023 theorem. Model transfer, one-sided success and parameter dependence were individually verified on 2026-09-16. The original extraction did not require deterministic algorithms, so the published randomized FPT result answers it. No Lean formalization is claimed.

importance.reason: The case of three terminal pairs was the missing boundary between the tractable two-pair case and W[1]-hard four-pair case in directed multicut. Its resolution clarifies a central parameterized separation problem and connects directed cuts to structural constraint complexity.
importance.basis: Individual review of survey Open Problem 3.4 and the resolving SODA 2023 theorem and proof. The historical significance is retained despite retirement from the open benchmark.

sentences: The problem asks to delete at most a prescribed number of arcs and destroy three specified directed reachability relations.
Its parameter is the cut size, while the number of terminal pairs is fixed at three.
The historical question was whether this case admits fixed-parameter algorithms, between two-pair tractability and four-pair hardness.
Hatzel and coauthors settled it positively with a randomized algorithm published at SODA 2023.
The complete record is retained in the archive, with weighted variants and deterministic derandomization kept separate from the resolved target.

definitions: The input is an unweighted finite directed graph \(D=([n],E)\), \(n\ge1\), with \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\), three ordered terminal pairs \((s_i,t_i)\in[n]^2\), and an integer \(0\le k\le |E|\). Loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc are unnecessary. Terminals may coincide. A directed path includes a path of length zero from a vertex to itself; an instance with \(s_i=t_i\) is therefore a NO instance. A feasible cut is a set \(S\subseteq E\) with \(|S|\le k\) such that for each \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\) no directed path from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) remains in \(D-S\). The requirements concern only the three specified directions, not every ordered pair among the terminals. No vertices are deleted. The input encoding consists of \(1^n0\), the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order, six terminal indices in binary blocks of length \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and \(k\) in a block of length \(\lceil\log_2(n^2+1)\rceil\). Use a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program for all valid inputs, independent fair random bits, no advice, and unit cost for each transition. All preprocessing and arithmetic count. It outputs either a list encoding a feasible cut or a failure symbol. On NO instances it must always output failure; on YES instances its success probability, over its own random bits, is at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds on every random tape. The function \(h\) depends only on \(k\); the polynomial exponent \(c\) is independent of \(k\). No specific exponential base, polynomial bound on \(h\), optimal cut or derandomization is required.
answer_criterion: The historical affirmative target is a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of correctness, the stated one-sided success guarantee and the \(h(k)(n+1)^c\) worst-case running time for a total computable \(h\). A complete Lean-checked negation of that existence statement would be the alternative answer. The checked published algorithm already answers the mathematical question affirmatively; this archival record does not claim that its proof has been formalized in Lean.

context_blocks.text: The survey asks for the parameterized complexity of exactly three directed terminal pairs in the edge-deletion model. This card records its tractability branch, including randomized algorithms, rather than imposing a new deterministic-only or single-exponential requirement.

Hatzel, Jaffke, Lima, Masařík, Pilipczuk, Sharma and Sorge prove fixed-parameter tractability with a randomized algorithm in Theorem 1.1. Their formal version permits undeletable vertices; the standard relation between arc and vertex deletion makes the result apply to this edge-deletion question.

The theorem is a one-sided search algorithm: every returned set is a valid solution, and a fixed existing solution survives the randomized part with a probability bounded below by a positive function of the parameter. The resulting success probability can be made a fixed constant within fixed-parameter time. This does not establish a deterministic algorithm.

The result concerns unweighted cuts. The same paper proves hardness for a weighted two-pair variant, so weights cannot be added to the statement without changing its classification. Its parameter dependence is not stated as a simple explicit exponential bound.
